strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely question: can LLMs improve reasoning using only intrinsic signals, without verifiable rewards? The proposed RLIF framing and INTUITOR method (replacing GRPO's external reward with self-certainty) is simple, elegant, and directly tests a critical assumption in the field.

The central empirical claim is well-supported: INTUITOR matches GRPO on in-domain math (GSM8K, MATH500) while transferring better to out-of-domain code tasks (LCB, CRUXEval), using no gold answers at all. The cross-model validation (Qwen 1.5B–14B, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.2, OLMo-2) is unusually thorough for this line of work.

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: the online vs. offline self-certainty comparison (Fig. 7) gives a concrete reward-hacking example and explains why co-evolving the reward with the policy prevents exploitation; the Mann–Whitney U analysis (Fig. 8) quantifies how well self-certainty separates correct from incorrect responses; the qualitative tracing of emergent pre-code reasoning (Fig. 6, Appendix B.5/B.6) is informative.

The paper includes sensible negative controls that many similar papers omit: random-reward baseline and entropy-minimization baseline both collapse, showing the gains are non-trivial; GRPO-PV (plurality voting) is included as an unsupervised RLVR-style comparator; KL-penalty ablation (Table 3) honestly documents hyperparameter sensitivity on out-of-domain tasks.

The observation that INTUITOR teaches a degenerate 1.5B model to produce coherent reasoning chains, and that gains emerge in instruction-following (AlpacaEval) without being targeted, is a genuinely interesting finding about latent behavioral priors in pretrained models.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited. The method is essentially a plug-in replacement of GRPO's reward with an existing confidence metric (self-certainty from Kang et al. 2025), and the 'RLIF' framing largely repackages concurrent intrinsic-reward work (EMPO, EM-RL, SEED-GRPO, TTRL, Genius). The technical contribution is a careful empirical study rather than a new algorithmic idea.

The 'matches GRPO' claim needs qualification. On the main 3B model, INTUITOR is consistently slightly below GRPO on in-domain math (0.792 vs 0.826 GSM8K; 0.612 vs 0.636 MATH500), and gains on Llama and OLMo are marginal or within noise (Table 5, Table 6). The stronger claim of parity really holds only for Qwen models and larger scales, and no statistical significance or multiple-seed variance is reported anywhere.

There is a fundamental unresolved question: is INTUITOR learning new reasoning capability or merely eliciting/cleaning up existing capabilities while making outputs more self-consistent and better formatted? The length increases (Fig. 3), format changes (Fig. 5), and instruction-following gains suggest format/elicitation effects that are not fully disentangled from genuine reasoning improvement. No contamination or capability-probing analysis is provided.

Heavy sensitivity to hyperparameters undermines the scalability story: larger models required a different system prompt, 10x smaller learning rate, and larger group size to avoid behavioral collapse (Appendix A.1), described as a 'first, untuned trial'; the KL ablation shows out-of-domain performance varies substantially with β (LCB ranges 0.081–0.153). It is unclear how much of the reported OOD advantage over GRPO survives careful tuning of either method.

Some analyses are thin: Fig. 6's output-type taxonomy is based on only ten randomly selected LiveCodeBench questions; the 'emergent reasoning' mechanism (Section 5.3) is largely speculative; the offline exploitation example is a single anecdote with a reduced batch size.

Reproducibility gaps: no explicit code/data release statement; evaluation relies on a GPT-4.1 judge for AlpacaEval; some inconsistencies between the text and tables (e.g., stated KL penalty β=0.005 in Section 4 vs. 0.0005 in Table 7; learning rate 3e-5 in text vs 3e-6 in Table 7) create confusion about the actual configuration.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether LLMs can improve reasoning using only intrinsic, self-generated signals, with a simple, general answer (replacing verifiable rewards in GRPO with self-certainty). The method is a one-line change to an existing pipeline, which makes it easy to understand and adopt.

Comprehensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: comparisons against GRPO (gold answers), GRPO-PV (plurality voting), entropy minimization, and random rewards; multiple backbone models (Qwen2.5 1.5B/3B/7B/14B, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.2-3B, OLMo-2-7B-SFT); multiple benchmark categories (math, code, instruction following).

Unusually careful analysis for this area: (i) the online vs. offline self-certainty experiment in Section 5.4 directly probes reward hacking and identifies a concrete failure mode (appending auxiliary solved problems) that the online annotator avoids; (ii) Mann-Whitney U analysis of self-certainty distributions on correct vs. incorrect responses; (iii) KL-penalty ablations showing out-of-domain sensitivity; (iv) negative controls showing entropy minimization collapses to repetition and random rewards degrade the model.

Interesting empirical findings beyond the headline claim: improved out-of-domain generalization (LCB, CRUXEval) relative to GRPO, emergence of structured pre-code reasoning, and rescue of a degenerate 1.5B base model, supported by qualitative rollout traces in the appendix.

Good reproducibility posture: shared hyperparameters for the GRPO comparison, full hyperparameter tables, system prompts, and example completions provided; standard frameworks (Open-R1, TRL, lighteval, ZeroEval, AlpacaEval 2.0 LC) used throughout.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the core method is GRPO with a swapped reward signal using an existing metric (self-certainty from Kang et al., 2025), and closely related concurrent work exists (EMPO, EM-RL, Prabhudesai et al.'s confidence maximization). The framing of 'RLIF' as a new paradigm overstates what is essentially a confidence-based unsupervised reward.

The mechanism behind the reported gains is not fully pinned down. The claim that rewarding the trajectory (rather than the outcome) explains better generalization is plausible but speculative; the paper does not disentangle whether OOD gains come from longer, reasoning-augmented outputs or genuinely improved code ability. The emergent-reasoning analysis (Figure 6) is based on only ten randomly selected questions, which is anecdotal.

In-domain results are slightly worse than GRPO on most settings (e.g., 0.792 vs. 0.826 GSM8K, 0.612 vs. 0.636 MATH500 for 3B), so 'matches GRPO' should be qualified; no variance/std over seeds is reported for any headline result, and single runs make small gaps hard to interpret.

Scale and duration of training are modest (58-117 steps, 7.5k problems), hyperparameters appear tuned per setting (different LR/KL/group sizes across model sizes and INTUITOR-Code), and the appendix admits the 7B/14B recipe required ad hoc stabilization with no systematic sweep, which weakens claims of scalability.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: phrases like 'transformative potential of RLIF' and autonomous self-improvement beyond human oversight are not supported by the experiments; the paper would benefit from more tempered framing and a clearer discussion of the limits of confidence-based rewards (e.g., behavior on tasks where high confidence and correctness are weakly correlated).

strengths: The core idea is simple and compelling: replacing verifiable rewards in GRPO with the model's own self-certainty yields a fully unsupervised RL recipe (INTUITOR) that matches gold-answer GRPO on in-domain math while generalizing better to out-of-domain code and instruction-following tasks. This directly addresses a real scalability bottleneck of RLVR.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad for a method paper: Qwen2.5-1.5B/3B/7B/14B, Qwen3-14B, Llama-3.2-3B, and OLMo-2-7B, with consistent baselines (GRPO, GRPO-PV following TTRL) and multiple evaluation axes (math, code, MMLU-Pro, AlpacaEval).

The analysis goes beyond headline numbers: the online-vs-offline self-certainty comparison (Figure 7) elegantly demonstrates and explains a concrete reward-hacking failure mode for a fixed annotator, and the Mann-Whitney analyses (Figure 8) support the claim that the online signal better separates correct from incorrect responses.

Appendix ablations are informative and honest: KL-penalty sensitivity (Table 3), entropy-minimization and random-reward controls showing degeneration, and documentation of behavioral collapse when naively scaling to 7B+, with the mitigations disclosed rather than hidden.

The qualitative analysis of emergent pre-code reasoning and output-type evolution (Figures 5-6, Appendix B) provides mechanistic intuition for why a confidence reward improves transfer, which is a genuinely interesting finding in its own right.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited relative to concurrent work. The method is essentially 'GRPO with an existing confidence metric (self-certainty from Kang et al., 2025) as reward,' and Prabhudesai et al. (cited only as a URL reference) and other concurrent label-free RL efforts (EMPO, EM-RL, TTRL) explore very similar territory. The RLIF framing is useful, but the delta over these works is not sharply delineated experimentally (e.g., no head-to-head comparison with entropy-based or EMPO-style intrinsic rewards in the main results).

In-domain, INTUITOR is consistently slightly below gold-answer GRPO (e.g., 0.792 vs 0.826 GSM8K, 0.612 vs 0.636 MATH500 at 3B), so the headline claim of 'matching' GRPO should be tempered; the paper's strongest evidence is on transfer, and even there the gains on some model families (Llama, OLMo) are marginal.

No variance reporting: results appear to be single training runs with no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests on the main benchmarks. Given that GRPO-style RL is notoriously high-variance and some reported differences (e.g., LCB 0.153 vs 0.085) hinge on such runs, statistical robustness is not established.

There is a plausible confound the paper does not fully rule out: self-certainty is a trajectory-level signal that correlates with response length/format, so some of the transfer gains may reflect longer, better-formatted outputs rather than improved reasoning. The length analysis (Figure 3) shows INTUITOR yields systematically longer completions; a length-matched or formatting-controlled evaluation would strengthen the causal claim.

Hyperparameter sensitivity is acknowledged (KL penalty strongly affects out-of-domain results) and larger models required an ad hoc recipe change (different LR, group size, system prompt, β), raising questions about whether 'INTUITOR' is one method or several hand-tuned configurations; a sweep or at least a justification for the chosen values is missing.

Some writing overclaims: statements about 'transformative potential,' autonomous superhuman self-improvement, and 'unlock rich latent capabilities' are not supported by the experiments, and the mechanism of why confidence maximization improves correctness remains hypothesis-level ('may contribute', 'potentially improving').

strengths: Clear and compelling research question: replacing external verifiable rewards with purely intrinsic confidence signals for RL on LLMs is timely and significant, given the domain-specificity and cost of RLVR verifiers.
The core method (INTUITOR) is simple and elegant: swapping GRPO's reward with a self-certainty score requires minimal implementation change, making it easy to adopt and reproduce.

Comprehensive evaluation: multiple model scales (1.5B–14B), multiple model families (Qwen, Llama, OLMo), multiple benchmarks (math, code, instruction following), and a strong label-free baseline (GRPO-PV / plurality voting from TTRL) to contextualize results.

Thoughtful analysis beyond headline numbers: (1) the online vs. offline self-certainty comparison convincingly shows the fixed-annotator reward is exploited while the co-evolving online reward is not; (2) the reward-exploitation analysis via Mann-Whitney tests on self-certainty distributions; (3) ablations against entropy minimization, random rewards, and log-prob rewards, demonstrating these alternatives collapse while self-certainty remains stable.

Honest reporting of limitations: sensitivity to KL penalty and hyperparameters, failure cases (Llama base model, larger model collapse requiring prompt/LR changes), and explicit acknowledgment that self-certainty is a weaker signal than true correctness.
The finding that INTUITOR generalizes better OOD than GRPO while slightly lagging in-domain is a genuinely interesting empirical observation with useful discussion of training-dynamics explanations.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the method is essentially GRPO with an existing confidence metric (Kang et al., 2025) substituted as the reward; the paper builds heavily on prior self-certainty work and sits among many concurrent unsupervised-RL papers (EMPO, Seed-GRPO, entropy rewards, Genurs, TTRL). The contribution is primarily an empirical demonstration, not a new algorithmic or theoretical idea.

Potential length-bias confound is not fully disentangled. Self-certainty (KL to uniform) inherently favors longer, more elaborate outputs, and Figures 3/9 show INTUITOR produces substantially longer responses than GRPO. The better OOD results (LCB, CRUX) may partly reflect longer/structured outputs rather than superior reasoning; a length-controlled analysis or pass@k comparison is missing.

No statistical reliability measures for the main results: single training runs, no seeds/variance reporting, no significance tests on the headline benchmark numbers. Gaps like GSM8K 0.792 vs 0.826 (GRPO) or MATH500 0.612 vs 0.636 are within plausible run-to-run variance, weakening claims of 'matching' GRPO.

Fragility of the approach is significant: larger models collapse with the default recipe and require ad-hoc fixes (simplified prompt, reduced LR, larger group size); the system prompt is acknowledged as a strong unexamined confound. This raises scalability concerns despite the abstract's framing of a 'scalable alternative to RLVR.'

In-domain performance consistently trails GRPO (e.g., Qwen2.5-3B: 0.612 vs 0.636 on MATH500; GSM8K 0.792 vs 0.826), and OLMo-2 results show essentially no gain over GRPO (and slightly worse on CRUX). The claim of parity is stronger than the evidence in some settings.

The 'emergent long-form reasoning' and instruction-following analyses are largely qualitative (10 randomly selected questions in Figure 6; anecdotal examples in the appendix), which limits the strength of the behavioral claims.

Missing comparison with some relevant baselines, e.g., direct best-of-n / self-consistency selection at inference time or other confidence-based selection methods, which would clarify whether RL training adds value over simply sampling and selecting by self-certainty at test time.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question: whether LLMs can be improved via RL without external verifiers or gold labels, with potential significance for domains where verifiable rewards are hard to construct.

The core experimental finding is interesting: a confidence-based intrinsic reward can roughly match GRPO on in-domain math benchmarks and, in some cases, transfer better to out-of-domain tasks (e.g., LiveCodeBench, CRUXEval).

The paper includes a fairly broad set of ablations in the appendix (KL penalty sensitivity, model scaling to 7B/14B, other model families like Llama-3.2 and OLMo-2, entropy-minimization and random-reward baselines, direct vs. policy-gradient optimization of self-certainty), and the analysis of online vs. offline self-certainty annotators and reward hacking is a nice touch.
Writing and overall structure are clear, and the method is simple and easy to reproduce conceptually.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the central ingredient (self-certainty, defined as KL from a uniform distribution to the model's next-token distribution) is taken directly from Kang et al. (2025), and the method is essentially 'GRPO with the reward swapped for a known confidence metric.' The 'RLIF' framing rebrands a straightforward substitution as a new paradigm; several concurrent works (EMPO, Seed-GRPO, entropy rewards, TTRL with plurality voting) occupy nearly the same design space, and the paper does not clearly differentiate INTUITOR's contribution beyond metric choice.

Headline claim is overstated relative to the evidence: on in-domain tasks INTUITOR mostly matches (often slightly trails) GRPO (e.g., 0.792 vs. 0.826 GSM8K; 0.612 vs. 0.636 MATH500), and GRPO-PV—a self-consistency-based, label-free baseline—performs comparably or better. This weakens the practical case for self-certainty specifically over simpler unsupervised alternatives, and the comparison to TTRL-style methods is superficial.

Evaluation rigor is insufficient for the claims made: results appear to be from single training runs with no error bars, seed variance, or statistical significance tests on benchmark accuracies (the Mann-Whitney tests concern self-certainty score separation, not accuracy differences). Many reported gaps (e.g., 0.612 vs. 0.612 vs. 0.636) are within plausible run-to-run variance.

There is an unaddressed confound: self-certainty is strongly correlated with response length and verbosity. Figures 3 and 13 show INTUITOR induces notably longer completions, and 'length-controlled' evidence is only provided for AlpacaEval via an LLM judge (GPT-4.1) with no human evaluation. The paper does not rule out that some gains (especially out-of-domain transfer) come from producing longer, more self-explanatory outputs rather than better reasoning.

The mechanistic story is speculative: claims of 'emergent structured reasoning' and 'the model practicing to become more confident' rest on qualitative inspection of ten randomly selected LiveCodeBench questions and a small output-type classification, not a controlled analysis.

Scalability and generality of the paradigm remain open: the method requires careful, per-model hyperparameter retuning (different learning rates, KL penalties, prompts per model size), larger models exhibit 'severe behavioral collapse' requiring undocumented fixes, and offline self-certainty training demonstrably degrades. This tempers the 'scalable alternative to RLVR' claim.

Some presentation issues: the code-availability statement in the abstract is incomplete ('Code is available at' with no link), Table 1 mixes different training data/hyperparameters for INTUITOR-Code, and the claim that INTUITOR 'matches GRPO' is contradicted in places by the paper's own numbers.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated research question: whether LLMs can improve reasoning using only intrinsic, self-generated reward signals, with the RLIF framing cleanly positioned relative to RLHF and RLVR.
Simple, elegant method: replacing verifiable rewards in GRPO with self-certainty (KL to uniform) requires minimal implementation change and no gold labels, making it broadly applicable.

Comprehensive empirical validation: multiple model families (Qwen, Llama, OLMo), model scales up to 14B, multiple domains (math, code, instruction following), and a GRPO-PV plurality-voting baseline that also avoids gold answers.

Thoughtful analysis of failure modes: the online vs. offline self-certainty comparison (Fig. 7) demonstrates reward exploitation of a static annotator and shows the online variant prevents reward hacking; comparison against entropy-minimization, random-reward, and log-probability baselines (Appendix B.4) convincingly shows the gains are non-trivial and that alternative intrinsic signals collapse.

Extensive ablations in the appendix (KL penalty, rollout size, direct optimization vs. policy gradient, sequential cross-domain training), along with released code, prompts, and hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility.
Interesting qualitative findings, e.g., emergence of structured pre-reasoning and improved self-assessment of correct vs. incorrect answers (Fig. 8).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the self-certainty metric is adopted directly from Kang et al. (2025) and the optimization machinery is standard GRPO; the contribution is primarily an empirical demonstration that this existing metric works as a reward, and several concurrent works (EMPO, Seed-GRPO, Genios, TTRL) explore very similar territory.
No theoretical grounding for why self-certainty is a good reward signal; the paper acknowledges this, but the mechanism connecting confidence maximization to accuracy remains largely speculative.

A potential confound is not fully resolved: self-certainty rewards likely correlate with response length and format, and the analysis of longer, more detailed reasoning outputs (Fig. 3) suggests gains may partly come from stylistic/instruction-following improvements rather than genuine reasoning gains. The GRPO-PV baseline partially addresses this but the distinction is not rigorously tested (e.g., no length-controlled or format-matched comparison).

Evaluation scope is modest: training on a single 7.5K-problem dataset (MATH), relatively small models, and no statistical significance/variance reporting for the main results in Table 1; some OOD gains over GRPO-PV are small and could be within noise.

The method requires a suitable question distribution and adequate prior domain knowledge in the base model (as the authors concede in B.10, e.g., failure on Llama3.2-3B-Base and sensitivity to hyperparameters), which limits the claimed generality of 'unsupervised' learning.
Claims of better OOD generalization than GRPO are somewhat overstated relative to the evidence: comparisons to the strongest baselines and larger-scale verification are incomplete.
